newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian employment growth seen staying weak.
newsitem.headline: Australian employment growth seen staying weak.

text.p: Australia's stagnant labour market is expected to have shown little signs of improvement in July, but economists said Thursday's data are unlikely to add much to the case for a further cut in interest rates.

While a rise in July employment is expected, unemployment is also expected to have risen, reflecting the subdued nature of the jobs market that has been a key influence on the five Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) rate cuts over the past year.
The median forecast of the 28 economists Reuters surveyed was for a 25,000 rise in July employment.
Forecasts range from a rise of 12,000 to a rise of 50,000.

"While we expect a bounceback in July as part of a continued rebound from the sharp fall in May, the underlying trend in the labour market will remain weak," Hambros fixed income economist Su-Lin Ong said.

Despite the expected employment rise, the unemployment rate is expected to edge back up to 8.6 percent, after dipping to 8.5 percent in June. This would be the 13th consecutive month where the unemployment rate has been 8.5 percent or higher.
Employment rose a disappointing 11,900 in June, when forecasts had centred on a 40,000 rise.
A 25,000 rise in July would mean that employment would have only caught up with what it was expected to have done in June, and would mean the labour market has been flat since April.
It would also mean that over the first seven months of 1997, employment had grown by an average of just 3,000 jobs per month.

Economists would also be looking at the composition of any jobs growth -- so far over 1997 full time employment has fallen by almost 64,000 while part-time employment has risen by 60,000. Full time jobs are seen as more beneficial to economic gorwth, as they give consumers greater spending power, they are seen as more permanent and they also have a greater impact on confidence, economists said.

Against a backdrop of low inflation, the stalled labour market has been a key factor behind the Reserve Bank of Australia's decision to cut official interest rates five times over the past year, most recently last week.
And while a result in line with expectations would add to emerging calls for a sixth cut in rates, most economists see that as unlikely at this stage.

Another weak jobs figure would not necessarily be a strong argument for another rate cut, despite softness in building approvals and retail trade data last week, and an expected fall in Friday's housing finance data, they said.
The first RBA rate cut was on July 31 last year.

As monetary policy is seen operating with a lag of 12 to 18 months, and employment is seen as a lagging indicator of a broader pick up in activity, economists said it was now time to allow the impact of the rate cuts to flow through to the economy.

"Monetary stimulus takes time to fully impact on business activity and employment growth," ANZ Investment Bank economists said in a commentary, adding the effects in the cuts over the past year were not likely to be fully realised until late 1998.

"Eventually, the RBA will believe that it has done all that can be reasonably expected of it. That point has probably been reached," they said, rating the chance of a sixth rate cut at no more than 40 percent.
Given these lags, some further weak labour force statistics would not be enough to justify a cut.
If, however, there were no signs of improvement by year end, then a sixth cut would become more likely, economists said.
"If growth fails to pick up as expected, another official rate cut cannot be ruled out -- particularly in the absence of other policy responses to high unemployment," Macquarie bank economists said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
